split.label: Pinned left
split.hint: The left side holds still and moves with you; the right column scrolls.

splitR.label: Pinned right
splitR.hint: The right side holds still and moves with you; the left column scrolls.

index.label: Live index
index.hint: An index follows you down the left while each specimen takes a full screen.

counter.label: Counter-scroll
counter.hint: Two columns drift in opposite directions as you scroll.

rail.label: Sideways rail
rail.hint: Scrolling down drives a track sideways past a fixed panel.

stack.label: Sticky stack
stack.hint: Specimens pile up like a deck of cards.

orbit.label: Centre stage
orbit.hint: A still centre; specimens arrive from both sides.

spine.label: Spine
spine.hint: A line fills as you scroll and specimens branch from it.

wheel.label: Carousel
wheel.hint: Specimens ride a ring that turns with the page.

tunnel.label: Fly-through
tunnel.hint: The camera moves forward through a column of specimens.

slides.label: Wipes
slides.hint: One specimen at a time, cut in by a moving edge.

columns.label: Parallax
columns.hint: Columns move at different speeds beside a fixed panel.

map.label: Pan map
map.hint: The page pans across a large field along a path.

canvas.label: Canvas flight
canvas.hint: The page is a canvas: scrolling pulls the camera out, flies it left, right, up or down to the next specimen, and drops it back in.

atlas.label: Atlas
atlas.hint: Every specimen sits on one sheet. The camera dives into each, and at the end of every row pulls right out to show the whole sheet.

spiral.label: Spiral
spiral.hint: The specimens wind outward in a spiral and the camera follows them round, banking as it turns.

families.title: Switchboard
families.line: Forty ways to flip a state.
families.blurb: Switches, latches and breakers on a canvas the camera flies across.
families.description: 01 · SWITCHBOARD — forty ways to flip a state.The still side is the board itself: forty lamps, one per specimen, thatlight as the page passes them while a scan line sweeps the grid.

families.title: Dials
families.blurb: Knobs, wheels and rotaries wound out along a spiral.
families.description: 02 · DIALS — turn, wind, spin and detent.The still centre is a dial of its own: a bezel that turns two full revolutionsagainst a needle that sweeps the other way, with an arc that draws as you go.

families.title: Faders
families.line: Sliders on a rail that slides.
families.blurb: Ranges, scrubbers and tracks on a sideways rail.
families.description: 03 · FADERS — sliders on a rail that slides.The still side is an eight-channel desk whose caps ride the scroll.

families.title: Keypads
families.line: Keys, triggers and buttons with a feel.
families.blurb: Press mechanics in three parallax columns.
families.description: 04 · KEYPADS — keys, triggers and buttons with a feel.The still side is a backlit key matrix; a wave of light and a press travelsacross it as the page scrolls.

families.title: Fields
families.blurb: Text, date, code and tag fields beside a live index.
families.description: 05 · FIELDS — inputs, pickers and steppers, reimagined.The still side is a form that fills itself in, row by row, as you read.

families.title: Gauges
families.blurb: Needles, arcs and bars wound out along a spiral.
families.description: 06 · GAUGES — meters that read the room.The pinned side is a dial stack that the scroll alone drives: three arcs fillat different rates, a ring of dashes turns, a needle trembles toward 100, andthe number in the middle is written by CSS counters — no script per frame.Angles throughout run clockwise from twelve o'clock.

families.title: Charts
families.blurb: Forty small charts on one sheet; the camera dives into each.
families.description: 07 · CHARTS — marks, bars, lines and areas.The still middle of the page is a plotter: a line is drawn down the screen asyou scroll, two series, a crosshair and a dot per series — the dots and thenumbers beside them come from the same sine sums the paths were drawn with, soCSS (sin, counters) and SVG agree without any script per frame.Every sample is generated from a seed, so a chart is the same on every render.

families.title: Matrices
families.line: Heat, tables and dot grids to pan across.
families.blurb: Heat, tables and dot grids on one sheet you fly across.
families.description: 08 · MATRICES — heat, tables and dot grids to pan across.The page is a field of forty-two grids you travel across along a snaking path.On the left, a small map of that field: the red cell and the dot are where thescroll has taken you, the line is the way so far, and the numbers beside themare written by CSS counters — the same `--pin` that moves the field draws them.Most specimens below are grids read with the pointer or the arrow keys(useCell); the rest are small games, tables and displays.

families.title: Figures
families.line: Numerals that roll, flip and settle.
families.blurb: Counters and clocks cut in one at a time.
families.description: 09 · FIGURES — numerals that roll, flip and settle.One specimen fills the right of the screen at a time, cut in by a moving edge.On the left, two odometers read the scroll itself: the big one counts whichspecimen you are on, the small one how far down the page you are. They arerolling reels of digits moved by CSS (round / mod on the scroll number), withthe carry behaving like a real odometer: a digit only turns over while theone beside it is passing nine.

families.title: Graphs
families.line: Nodes, trees and flows that grow.
families.blurb: Networks that branch from a filling spine.
families.description: 10 · GRAPHS — nodes, trees and flows that grow.A spine runs down the middle of the page and specimens branch off it. The discthat rides the spine is a graph of its own: thirty-one nodes appear one by oneas you scroll, each link drawing itself from its parent, and the counters inthe middle are written by CSS. Everything below is a graph of some kind —trees, networks, flows, fractals — drawn from fixed data, so it is the sameon every render.

families.title: Kinetic
families.line: Words that scramble, split and settle.
families.blurb: Moving type on a canvas the camera swoops across.
families.description: 11 · KINETIC — words that scramble, split and settle.The still side is one enormous letter. As you scroll it steps through thealphabet, and between two letters each is cut in half across the middle: thehalves slide apart in opposite directions as one fades out and the next slidestogether. The numbers that drive it are the page's --f, read by CSS.Everything below is a line of moving type; the ones that react to the pointerwork from the keyboard too.

families.title: Tickers
families.blurb: Mechanical text on belts that slide both ways.
families.description: 12 · TICKERS — flaps, boards and marquees.The still side is a split-flap board. Every flap is a scroll-driven counter:CSS reads the page's --pin, turns it into "which letter, and how far throughthe flip", prints the letters with counters (upper-alpha, decimal) and tiltsthe two moving halves by that fraction. Nothing is animated by script.Everything on the right is a belt, a board or a sign.

families.title: Markup
families.blurb: Annotations that stack like pages in a deck.
families.description: 13 · MARKUP — highlights, strikes and redactions.The still side is a page of notes. As you scroll, a pen goes through it: aphrase is highlighted, another crossed out, a word circled, a few lines blackedout. Each mark has a progress of its own (--m, from the page's --pin and themark's order) and CSS draws it; nothing is animated by script.Everything in the deck is something you can do to a line of text.

families.title: Glyphs
families.blurb: Letterforms riding a carousel ring.
families.description: 14 · GLYPHS — outlines, strokes and letterforms.The still side is a type specimen sheet: one huge glyph at a time, drawnagainst the five lines every letter lives between (ascender, cap height,x-height, baseline, descender). The scroll outlines the glyph, then a scanline fills it from the top; the next glyph takes over. The metrics are thereal ones for the site's serif. Everything is CSS reading the page's --pin.The ring carries forty-two things you can do to a letter.

families.title: Editorial
families.blurb: Editorial parts met on a fly-through.
families.description: 15 · EDITORIAL — quotes, captions and footnotes.The still side is a magazine page that sets itself as you scroll: a kicker,a headline that rises line by line, a standfirst that wipes in, two columns oftext filling line by line, a pull quote, a figure, a footnote. Each part has awindow of the scroll and CSS reads it from the page's --pin.What flies past is the furniture of a page of editorial.

families.title: Tilt
families.blurb: Parallax and tilt surfaces in a deep column.
families.description: 16 · TILT — cards with depth and weight.The still side is an exploded module in isometric view. Its six layers pullapart along the vertical axis and close again as you scroll, and the wholething turns a quarter: the gap is sin(pin × π), the turn is pin, both in CSS.Forty-two cards ride the fly-through, each doing something with perspective.

families.title: Glow
families.line: Spotlights, beams and borders of light.
families.blurb: Light-led cards on a dark canvas, found by flying across it.
families.description: 17 · GLOW — spotlights, beams and borders of light.The still side is a pendant lamp that swings over a row of tiles. Where thecone falls a tile lights up: border, fill, glow and lift. Both the swing and thecone are one number — the beam's position, sin(pin × 4π) — and CSS does therest (atan2 for the lamp's angle, a clip-path for the cone, clamp for how liteach tile is). Forty-two cards on the left are each lit in their own way.

families.title: Fold
families.line: Cards that flip, fold and peel.
families.blurb: Turning, folding cards on a rotating ring.
families.description: 18 · FOLD — cards that flip, fold and peel.The still side is a leaflet of four panels. Each panel hangs from the onebefore it, and each hinge turns by the same --fold (times 1, -2, 2: that is whatmakes it an accordion). The scroll opens it flat, holds it, and folds it theother way. The turning ring on the right holds forty-two things to flip, fold,peel and tear.

families.title: Bento
families.blurb: Dashboard tiles on one sheet, dived into one by one.
families.description: 19 · BENTO — tiles that tessellate.The still side is one board of eight tiles that settles into three differentarrangements as you scroll. Each tile has a rectangle in each arrangement, andits box is a blend of the three, weighted by two eased numbers taken from --pin:plain calc(), no script. On the right, forty-two dashboard tiles drift in twocolumns, each one a small working thing.

families.title: Passes
families.blurb: Perforated passes scattered over a canvas the camera flies across.
families.description: 20 · PASSES — tickets, receipts and badges.A line runs down the middle of the page and a pass hangs from either side of it.The medallion that rides the line is a pass of its own: a code prints itself rowby row as you scroll, a ring of forty-two punch holes fills one for each passyou have passed, and the counter in the middle is written by CSS. Everythingbelow is something you could be handed at a door — boarding passes to tear,stamps to land, codes to scan, badges to swing.

families.title: Tabs
families.line: Strips, pills and segments that glide.
families.blurb: Tab systems beside a live index.
families.description: 21 · TABS — strips, pills and segments that glide.The still side is a strip of five tabs whose underline is driven by thescroll alone: it slides along the strip, the label it reaches lights, and apanel title below it follows. Specimens share one small tablist (rovingtabindex, arrow keys, Home and End), so every one of them works from a keyboard.

families.title: Docks
families.blurb: Bars and rails on a canvas the camera flies across.
families.description: 22 · DOCKS — floating bars, rails and toolbars.The still side is a dock of seven discs with the classic magnification, butdriven by the scroll: a swell travels along the row as the page moves, sothe disc under the "cursor" rises and its neighbours follow.

families.title: Menus
families.blurb: Menu forms around a pinned node map.
families.description: 23 · MENUS — dropdowns, radials and command lists.The still side is a node map: a hub and seven stops joined by lines. Thescroll opens one stop at a time (a petal lifts and its line fills) while apulse runs out along the line to it. Specimens share a tiny open/close hook(Escape and an outside press close a menu) and are operable by keyboard.

families.title: Steps
families.blurb: Sequences along a sideways rail.
families.description: 24 · STEPS — steppers, breadcrumbs and pagination.The still side is a winding path: a line that draws itself as the pagescrolls, a marker that rides it, and five waypoints that light as it passes.Specimens share nothing but good manners: every stepper can be moved fromthe keyboard and says where it is in words.

families.title: Waypoints
families.blurb: Wayfinding pieces on an atlas you fly across.
families.description: 25 · WAYPOINTS — outlines, contents and wayfinding.The still side is a compass: a needle that turns twice over the journey andeight waypoints around the dial that light as it passes. Specimens are theother ways a page tells you where you are and where to go next.

families.title: Loaders
families.blurb: Spinners and waiting states wound out along a spiral.
families.description: 26 · LOADERS — forty ways to wait.Nearly everything here runs by itself, and only while it is on screen (thespecimen frame pauses every animation that is off-screen). The still side isa core with five rings that the scroll turns at five speeds, so the pageitself is the thing being waited on.

families.title: Toasts
families.blurb: Notices that arrive and pile up.
families.description: 27 · TOASTS — alerts, banners and notices.The still side is a stack of five notices that arrive one by one as the pagescrolls: each slides in on its --f and the ones before it shrink back, asa real stack does. Specimens use a small queue (auto-dismiss that pausesunder the pointer or focus) and announce themselves politely to a screen reader.

families.title: Progress
families.line: Bars, rings and vessels that fill.
families.blurb: Fills and meters in counter-scrolling columns.
families.description: 28 · PROGRESS — bars, rings and vessels that fill.Most specimens are pure CSS: one registered number, --prog-v (0 to 1), is run by akeyframe animation and every bar, ring and counter below reads it, so theyall fill in step with their own clock. The ones that answer to you are thesliders, the uploads and the buttons. The still side is a ring and three barsthat the scroll itself fills, with the figure written by CSS counters.

families.title: Skeletons
families.blurb: Waiting shapes cut in one at a time.
families.description: 29 · SKELETONS — placeholders and empty states.The still side is one card that resolves as you scroll: grey bars sharpeninto a heading, a line of text and a figure at the scroll's own pace (everystep is a CSS number, so nothing re-renders). Specimens are the waitingshapes — and what a page says when there is nothing to wait for.

families.title: Signals
families.blurb: Status lights beside a pinned beacon.
families.description: 30 · SIGNALS — lights, pills and health.The still side is a beacon whose colour is the scroll's progress: it goesfrom green to amber to red as the page is read, its rings widen and the wordunder it changes with it. Specimens are the other ways a thing can say howit is — and each one says it in words as well as in light.

families.title: Popovers
families.blurb: Anchored overlays with a pinned reference.
families.description: 31 · POPOVERS — tooltips, hover cards and callouts.The still side is a reference square with one popover that walks round it:the scroll sets its angle, so over the page it takes up every placement inturn, its arrow turning to keep pointing home. Specimens use a tiny open /close hook (Escape and an outside press close one) and every tooltip opens onkeyboard focus as well as on hover.

families.title: Sheets
families.blurb: Layered panes met on a fly-through.
families.description: 32 · SHEETS — drawers, modals and layered panes.The still side is a stack of five panes in depth: the scroll slides themapart along the view axis, each lifting out of the pile in turn, the waylayers come apart in a design tool. Every specimen lives in a small stage ofits own (so a "full screen" sheet only fills its box), traps nothing,and closes with its own button or Escape.

families.title: Cursors
families.blurb: Pointer effects across a canvas the camera flies over.
families.description: 33 · CURSORS — pointers, followers and magnets.Every specimen is an area that publishes two numbers, --x and --y (0 to 1,where the pointer is), and CSS does the rest — a follower is a transitionwith a lag, a trail is the same dot with longer lags, a magnet is atranslate. Nothing re-renders as the pointer moves. When nobody is pointing,a virtual pointer wanders on a slow curve (while the specimen is on screen,never under reduced motion) so the effect is always visible; the arrow keysmove it by hand.The still side is the same idea driven by the page: a cursor rides a figureof eight, trailing ghosts, as the scroll moves.

families.title: Wipes
families.blurb: Transitions cut in by a moving edge.
families.description: 34 · WIPES — curtains, clips and reveals.A wipe is a rule for how panel B replaces panel A, so nearly every specimenis the same two panels and a different rule. Press one to run it; untilsomeone does, each runs itself now and then while it is on screen (never underreduced motion). The still side is one wipe, scrubbed by the scroll: a clipedge sweeps across a pair of panels from first to last.

families.title: Lenses
families.blurb: Lenses on belts that slide both ways.
families.description: 35 · LENSES — magnifiers, compare and focus.A lens shows the same thing twice, once as it is and once changed, and letsthe pointer decide where. Most specimens publish the pointer as --x / --y(pointerVars.js) and draw a second, changed copy of the picture clipped toa shape that sits on it; a wandering virtual pointer keeps them moving untilyou take over. The still side is one lens that the scroll carries across apage of small type, enlarging whatever it passes.

families.title: Cockpit
families.blurb: Flight instruments on a rotating ring.
families.description: 36 · COCKPIT — instruments with presence.Sixteen of the forty-two are one dial component given sixteen faces (arange, a sweep, coloured bands, a redline): every needle can be dragged, anduntil you do, each wanders between readings by itself while it is on screen.The rest are the instruments a dial cannot be — a horizon, a compass card, alever, a tape. The still side is a heading card that the scroll turns twice.

families.title: Studio
families.line: Meters, reels and faders for sound.
families.blurb: Studio gear beside a pinned VU needle.
families.description: 37 · STUDIO — meters, reels and faders for sound.Nothing here makes a sound: these are the faces of studio gear. The stillside is a VU meter whose needle follows a swinging signal that the scrollscrubs — a loud passage, a quiet one, a peak. Specimens that would be movingin a studio move by themselves while on screen (never under reduced motion),and the ones you operate are real controls with values you can read.

families.title: Terminal
families.blurb: Console parts with a live index.
families.description: 38 · TERMINAL — pieces of a command line.Everything is drawn in text. The still side is a console window that printsa build log line by line as the scroll advances; the forty-two specimensbeside it are prompts, logs, diffs and menus. The ones that would be runningrun by themselves while on screen (never under reduced motion), and the onesthat take input are real inputs and buttons with the keys you would expect.

families.title: Stamps
families.blurb: Marks pressed onto a canvas, found one by one.
families.description: 39 · STAMPS — marks pressed onto paper: labels, seals, stickers and tape.The still side is a large APPROVED stamp coming down onto paper as thescroll advances (it lands at the middle of the page and the ink spreadsafter). The forty-two specimens are the things you would find on a desk:most can be pressed, peeled or torn with a click, and every one is a buttonor a field you can reach with the keyboard.

families.title: Archive
families.blurb: Records filed in a sticky deck.
families.description: 40 · ARCHIVE — files, drawers and index cards.The still side is a card drawer: a row of index cards that slides past asthe scroll advances, the one in front turning to face you. The forty-twospecimens are the furniture of a records room. Most of them open, pull out orturn over with a click; every one is a button or a field, so the keyboardreaches them all.

families.title: Beams
families.blurb: Light traces running along a spine.
families.description: 41 · BEAMS — lines and traces of light.The still side is a circuit trace that runs the length of the page: a pulseof light travels along it as the scroll advances and the pads it passes lightup behind it. The forty-two specimens are swatches of light on a dark ground:traces, tubes, rays and sweeps. The ones that would be moving are, while onscreen (never under reduced motion); the rest answer to the pointer, a dragor a click, and all of them can be reached from the keyboard.

families.title: Patterns
families.line: Grids, dots and hatching as surfaces.
families.blurb: Surfaces laid out on one sheet.
families.description: 42 · PATTERNS — grids, dots and hatching as surfaces.The still side is a sheet whose surface changes as the scroll advances: afield of dots grows, then gives way to hatching from the left. The forty-twospecimens are swatches. Thirty of them are drawn with nothing but gradientsand inline SVG tiles (so they cost no images); the rest move, follow thepointer or take a slider, and every control can be reached from the keyboard.

families.title: Drift
families.blurb: Particle systems wound out along a spiral.
families.description: 43 · DRIFT — particles, stars and rain.The still side is a spiral of dots that winds up as the scroll advances.Each of the forty-two specimens is a small particle system drawn on its owncanvas. A system only runs while it is on screen, and under reduced motion itdraws one settled frame and stops. Where the pointer matters it is thepointer (or the arrow keys, with Enter to act), so a keyboard reaches them all.

families.title: Waves
families.blurb: Wave forms on sliding belts.
families.description: 44 · WAVES — ripples, interference and noise.The still side is two sets of rings that spread apart as the scroll advances,so the pattern where they overlap shifts. Each of the forty-two specimens isa wave drawn on its own canvas through the shared Sim engine (Sim.jsx): itruns only while on screen, draws one settled frame under reduced motion, andwhere the pointer matters it is the pointer, or the arrow keys with Enter.

families.title: Morphs
families.blurb: Shape-changers scattered across a canvas.
families.description: 45 · MORPHS — shapes that become other shapes.The still side is one shape that is a circle at the top of the page, a star inthe middle and a square at the end, with every point of its outline slidingbetween them as the scroll advances. The forty-two specimens change shapetoo: by sliding the points of a clipped outline (the same trick), by CSSradii and transforms, by tweening the numbers of an SVG, or by meltingtogether through a blur-and-threshold filter. Each one changes when you click,hover or slide it, or by itself while on screen.

families.title: Handset
families.blurb: Phone-screen patterns beside a pinned handset.
families.description: 46 · HANDSET — mobile screens, from first run to settings.The still side is a phone whose screen slides through five states as thescroll advances: welcome, sign in, a feed, a chat and settings. Each of theforty-two specimens is a small screen of the same kind, drawn at phoneproportions: the ones you would tap are real buttons, fields and switchesthat work, and the ones that would run on their own do so while on screen.

families.title: Boards
families.blurb: Planning surfaces on one sheet.
families.description: 47 · BOARDS — kanban, calendars and agendas on one sheet.The still side is a three-lane board whose cards move across it as the scrolladvances: from To do, through Doing, to Done. The forty-two specimens areplanning surfaces of the same kind, small enough to sit on one sheet andworking: cards move when you click them, days and slots select, and theboards that would be ticking over (a countdown, a focus timer) do so whilethey are on screen.

families.title: Feeds
families.blurb: Streams and lists with a live index.
families.description: 48 · FEEDS — lists, chats and notification streams.The still side is a chat stream that scrolls past as the scroll advances,the message in the middle of the frame lit and the ones leaving it fadingout. The forty-two specimens are the parts of a stream: list rows you pick,reorder or expand, chat bubbles and their small furniture, and the ways anotification arrives and goes. Everything that takes input is a real buttonor field, and the streams that would be arriving do so while on screen.

families.title: Checkout
families.blurb: Sample pricing and order parts in parallax columns.
families.description: 49 · CHECKOUT — pricing, carts and order flows.The still side is a receipt that prints as the scroll advances: a lineappears for each item, then the total underlines itself. The forty-twospecimens are the parts of buying something: plan cards and toggles, cartlines and shipping, the steps of paying, and what comes after. The prices aremade up, but every control does its sum: change a quantity, a plan or a tipand the totals follow. Nothing is sent anywhere.

families.title: Heroes
families.blurb: Layouts for opening screens, scattered across a canvas.
families.description: 50 · HEROES — opening screens, bands and endings.The still side is one hero that re-lays itself out as the scroll advances:the headline slides left while a shape grows in on the right and the buttonsettles beneath. The forty-two specimens are layouts of the same kind, drawnsmall: openings of every shape, the bands that sit between sections, and theendings that close a page. Each has one thing you can do to it (press,type, hover, switch) or does something by itself while on screen.

entries.name: Calendar
entries.summary: A single-date calendar with roving focus, min/max bounds, month navigation and locale-aware labels.

props.name: label
props.description: Visible or accessible name. Keep it meaningful in the page context.

props.name: value
props.description: Selected ISO YYYY-MM-DD civil date.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Initial value for uncontrolled usage. Subsequent changes to defaultValue do not reset state.

props.name: onChange
props.description: Called when a day is selected, not when focus alone moves.

props.name: min
props.description: Lower bound: ISO date for date fields, percentage for split panels.

props.name: max
props.description: Upper bound in the same units as min.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables editing and activation.

props.name: locale
props.description: Intl locale for day names, month title and accessible dates.

props.name: weekStartsOn
props.description: First weekday, 0 = Sunday; default 0.

props.name: today

entries.description:
The label, hint and error every field shares, wired up so a screen reader
hears them: the control receives its id, `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid`
from the function passed as `children`.

<Field label="Email" hint="We reply from this address." error={error}>
 {(props) => <input {...props} type="email" />}
</Field>

An error replaces the hint, and is announced when it appears.

notes: An error replaces the hint, so the described-by pointer never points at something that is not there.

Every other input in the kit is built on this.

for the list, ← → (and Home, End) move between tabs and show the panel at once,

tabs: [{ id, label, content }]

First and last tab.
Leaves the list for the panel.

The content of panels that are not shown is not rendered at all, and their panel element is hidden.

entries.name: Toolbar
entries.summary: A row of tool buttons that is one tab stop; the arrow keys move between the tools. A tool can be a toggle, with aria-pressed.
entries.description:
A row of tool buttons that is one tab stop: ← → (and Home, End) move between
the tools, as the ARIA toolbar pattern asks. A tool with `toggle` is a pressed/
not-pressed button and says so with `aria-pressed`.

items: [{ id, label, icon: LucideIcon, toggle?, pressed?, onClick? } | { separator: true }]

props.name: label
props.description: Names the toolbar.

props.name: items
props.description: { id, label, icon?, toggle?, pressed?, onClick? } or { separator: true }.

keyboard.does: Move between tools, wrapping.
First and last tool.
Press the tool.
Leave the toolbar.

notes: Icon-only tools get their name from the label, which is also their tooltip.
Roving tabindex: only the tool you last used is in the tab order.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Toolbar label="Text formatting" items={[{ id: 'b', label: 'Bold', icon: Bold, toggle: true }, { id: 'i', label: 'Italic', icon: Italic, toggle: true }]} />

entries.name: Alert
entries.summary: A message in the flow of the page. Information and success speak politely; warnings and errors interrupt. The tone is never carried by colour alone.

props.name: tone
props.description: Sets the icon, the colour and how it is announced.

props.name: title
props.description: A short bold line.

props.name: children
props.description: The message.

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Adds a dismiss button when given.

keyboard.does: To the dismiss button, if there is one.

notes: role="status" for info and success, role="alert" for warning and danger.
Do not auto-dismiss an alert; use a Toast for something that needs no answer.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Alert tone="warning" title="Token expires soon">Replace it before Friday.</Alert>

entries.name: Banner
entries.summary: A notice that runs the width of its container, for something about the whole page or site rather than one field. It may carry one action and may be dismissed.

props.name: title
props.description: A bold lead-in.

props.name: action
props.description: { label, to } for a link or { label, onClick } for a button.

props.name: dismissible
props.description: Show a dismiss button.

keyboard.does: To the action, then to the dismiss button.

notes: A group named by its title, so two banners on a page never collide as landmarks.
Dismissal lasts until the page is reloaded; nothing is stored.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Banner title="New:" action={{ label: 'Read the notes', to: '/resources/changelog' }}>A chapter was added to the release notes.</Banner>

entries.name: EmptyState
entries.summary: What a list or a page says when there is nothing in it: why it is empty, and the one thing to do next. An empty state with no way forward is a dead end.

props.name: icon
props.description: A lucide icon.

props.name: title
props.description: A heading (level 3).

props.name: children
props.description: One or two sentences.

props.name: action
props.description: The next step, usually a button.

keyboard.does: To the action.

notes: Say why it is empty — “nothing yet” and “nothing matches your filter” need different words.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <EmptyState icon={CalendarX2} title="Nothing scheduled" action={<button>Add the first one</button>}>When a job is scheduled it appears here.</EmptyState>

entries.name: Meter
entries.summary: A gauge for a quantity inside a known range. The colour changes in the low and high zones and the zone is also written out for anyone who cannot see the colour.
entries.description:
A gauge for a quantity inside a known range (disk used, budget spent) — not
progress toward a goal, which is a ProgressBar. Drawn as cells; the colour
changes in the low and high zones, and the zone is also written out for
anyone who cannot see the colour. `role="meter"` carries the numbers.

props.name: label
props.description: What is measured.

props.name: value
props.description: The reading and its range.

props.name: min
props.description: The reading and its range.

props.name: max
props.description: The reading and its range.

props.name: low
props.description: Below low or above high changes the zone.

props.name: high
props.description: Below low or above high changes the zone.

props.name: cells
props.description: How many cells to draw; the unit after the number.

props.name: unit
props.description: How many cells to draw; the unit after the number.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

notes: role="meter" with min, max, now and a text value that includes the zone.
A meter is not progress toward a goal — that is a ProgressBar.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Meter label="Storage used" value={62} unit="%" low={10} high={85} />

entries.name: ProgressBar
entries.summary: How far along something is. With a value it announces its percentage; without one it is indeterminate and says it is working.

props.name: label
props.description: What is progressing; names the bar.

props.name: value
props.description: Omit value for indeterminate.

props.name: max
props.description: Omit value for indeterminate.

props.name: hideValue
props.description: Do not write the percentage beside the label.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

notes: role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuetext and a name.
Indeterminate stops moving under reduced motion.
For a quantity in a range (storage used), use Meter.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<ProgressBar label="Importing rows" value={42} />
<ProgressBar label="Waiting for the server" />

entries.name: Skeleton
entries.summary: The shape of content that has not arrived yet, holding its space so nothing jumps when it does. Decorative: hidden from assistive technology.
entries.description:
The shape of content that has not arrived yet. Purely decorative, so it is
hidden from assistive technology — pair it with a live "loading" message
(a Spinner with `hideLabel`) wherever the wait matters.

<Skeleton width="60%" height="1rem" />      one block
<Skeleton lines={3} />                      a short paragraph

props.name: width
props.description: CSS lengths.

props.name: height
props.description: CSS lengths.

props.name: lines
props.description: Draw a short paragraph instead of one block; the last line is shorter.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

notes: Pair it with a live “loading” message (a Spinner with hideLabel) wherever the wait matters.
The shimmer stops under reduced motion.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Skeleton width="48%" height="1.1rem" />
<Skeleton lines={3} />

entries.name: Spinner
entries.summary: A small “working on it” ring. It is a status message first — the label is announced — and a picture second. It stops turning for visitors who ask for less motion.

props.name: label
props.description: The words announced (and shown).

props.name: size
props.description: The ring’s size, as a CSS length.

props.name: hideLabel

<Spinner label="Saving" />
<Spinner label="Working" hideLabel />

entries.name: StatusDot
entries.summary: A coloured dot with its state spelled out beside it, so the colour is never the only signal. A live one can breathe.

props.name: state
props.description: Sets the colour and the default word.

props.name: label
props.description: The text beside the dot.

props.name: pulse
props.description: A slow ring for a live thing; stops under reduced motion.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

notes: The words are Operational, Degraded, Down and Idle unless you give your own.

examples.title: Basic usage

<StatusDot state="ok" pulse />
<StatusDot state="warn" label="Slow responses" />

entries.name: ToastProvider
entries.summary: Brief messages in a corner that leave by themselves. Announced politely, never take focus, pause while the pointer or keyboard is on them, and can always be dismissed.
entries.description:
Brief messages that appear in a corner and leave by themselves. They are
announced politely in a live region, never take focus, pause while the pointer
or keyboard is on them, and can always be dismissed. A toast is for something
that needs no answer ("Copied"); anything that does is a dialog.

props.name: title
props.description: The message.

props.name: body
props.description: The message.

props.name: tone
props.description: Icon and border.

props.name: duration
props.description: Milliseconds before it leaves; 0 keeps it until dismissed.

props.name: max (provider)
props.description: How many show at once; older ones leave first.

keyboard.does: To a toast’s dismiss button; focusing a toast stops its timer.

notes: A toast is for something that needs no answer. Anything that does is a dialog.
Outside a provider, useToast returns a function that does nothing — so a component that toasts never has to know.

entries.name: Badge

props.name: tone
props.description: The colour treatment.

props.name: dot

props.name: items
props.description: { label, value, display? }.

props.name: max

props.name: unit

props.description: Whether a toggle chip is on.

props.name: onClick

entries.name: CodeBlock
entries.summary: A block of code with an optional file name, light colouring and a copy button. The colour is a nicety: every token is also plain text, so copying gives exactly what you see.
entries.description:
A block of code with an optional file name, light colouring and a copy button.
The colours are a nicety: every token is also plain text, so copying gives you
exactly what you see, and the block is a focusable region so a keyboard user
can scroll a long line. `lines` adds line numbers.

props.name: code
props.description: The text.

props.name: language
props.description: js, jsx, ts, json, css, sh, html or yaml; anything else is shown plain.

props.name: filename
props.description: Shown in the header; also names the region.

props.name: lines
props.description: Number the lines (the numbers are not copied).

keyboard.does: To the copy button, then into the code, so a long line can be scrolled with the arrow keys.

notes: The colouring is deliberately small — a tokenizer of about eighty lines, no dependency.
Copying uses the clipboard API, with a fallback for browsers that do not offer it.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <CodeBlock filename="retry.js" lines code={source} />

entries.name: DataTable
entries.summary: A table you can sort and select from. A sortable column’s header is a button and the th carries aria-sort. It scrolls sideways inside a focusable region on a narrow screen.
entries.description:
A table you can sort and select from. A sortable column's header is a button
and the `th` carries `aria-sort`; the first press sorts ascending, the second
descending, the third restores the original order. The table scrolls sideways
inside a focusable region on a narrow screen rather than breaking the page.

columns: [{ key, label, sortable?, align?: 'right', render?: (row) => node, value?: (row) => sortable }]

props.name: caption
props.description: The table’s caption and the region’s name.

props.name: columns
props.description: { key, label, sortable?, align?, render?, value? }.

props.name: rows
props.description: Objects; each needs a unique rowKey.

props.name: selectable
props.description: Adds checkboxes; onSelect receives the chosen keys.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Adds checkboxes; onSelect receives the chosen keys.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Scroll vertically past this height; the header stays.

keyboard.does: On a header button: sort ascending, then descending, then back to the original order.
Into the scrolling region, then through its buttons and checkboxes.

notes: Sorting is stable and numeric-aware; numbers in a column should be right-aligned.
The header checkbox is indeterminate when only some rows are chosen.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <DataTable caption="Scheduled jobs" rows={rows} selectable onSelect={setChosen} columns={[{ key: 'job', label: 'Job', sortable: true }, { key: 'mins', label: 'Minutes', sortable: true, align: 'right' }]} />

props.name: items

props.name: stacked

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <DescriptionList items={[{ term: 'Service', detail: 'Order intake' }, { term: 'Owner', detail: 'Commerce team' }]} />

entries.name: Sparkline
entries.summary: A tiny line chart with no axes, for “which way is it going”. It is an image with a text description — range, first and last value — so the shape is never the only way to learn it.

props.name: data
props.description: At least two values.

props.name: label
props.description: Used in the text description.

props.name: width
props.description: The viewBox; the chart scales to its container.

props.name: height
props.description: The viewBox; the chart scales to its container.

props.name: unit
props.description: Used in the text description.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

entries.name: Stat
entries.summary: One number, large, with its label above and, if you have it, how it moved. The change is written as words for a screen reader; the arrow and colour are decoration.

props.name: label
props.description: The caption, the figure, and the small word after it.

props.name: value
props.description: The caption, the figure, and the small word after it.

props.name: unit
props.description: The caption, the figure, and the small word after it.

props.name: change
props.description: Percent change; positive, negative or zero.

props.name: changeLabel
props.description: What it is compared with.

props.name: note
props.description: A caveat or a source.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

notes: Figures use lining numerals, so a 1 never looks like a capital I.
Say what a figure is compared with, or leave the change off.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Stat label="Jobs on time" value="96" unit="%" change={2} changeLabel="vs. last week" />

entries.name: Table
entries.summary: Semantic table parts with optional sortable headers and a selected-row action group.

props.name: children
props.description: Content rendered in this part.

props.name: label
props.description: Visible or accessible name. Keep it meaningful in the page context.

keyboard.does: Focus the table scroll region, sorting controls and selected-row actions.
Activate sorting and action buttons.

rules: The table fills its named scroll region. Wide content scrolls within that region.
Table sections, rows and cells are measured inside a complete table, not as invalid standalone HTML.

notes: Keep native HTML nesting: Table → TableHeader/TableBody/TableFooter → TableRow → TableHeaderCell/TableCell.
TableHeaderCell becomes sortable only when onSort is supplied. The host passes sortDirection and changes its rows.
Use DataTable for a ready-made sortable/selectable table; use these parts when composing table hooks.
Selection state belongs to the host. TableSelectionToolbar calls onClear and renders any additional host actions.

Things in the order they happen, down a line. It is an ordered list, so the
order is announced; `when` can be a date, a phase or just "Step 3". Items with
`done` get a filled marker. The site's own timeline is told in undated phases —
pass words, not dates, unless you have them.

items: [{ when?, title, body?, done? }]

props.name: items

entries.name: Tree
entries.summary: An expandable tree — files, categories, an outline — following the ARIA tree-view pattern: one tab stop, arrow keys through what is visible.
entries.description:
An expandable tree (files, categories, an outline), following the ARIA tree-view
pattern: one tab stop; ↑ ↓ move through what is visible; → opens a closed
branch or steps into an open one; ← closes it or steps out to the parent; Home
and End jump; Enter or Space chooses. `onSelect` receives the node.

nodes: [{ id, label, children?: [...] }]

props.name: nodes
props.description: { id, label, children? }, nested to any depth.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Called with the chosen node.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Ids of branches that start open.

keyboard.does: Next or previous visible item.
Open a closed branch; on an open one, step into it.
Close an open branch; on a closed one or a leaf, step out to the parent.
First and last visible item.
Choose (and open or close) the item.

notes: aria-level, aria-setsize and aria-posinset are set, so a screen reader can say “3 of 5, level 2”.

examples.title: Basic usage

entries.name: useTableSortable
entries.summary: { rows, sort, setSort, toggleSort(key) }.
params: { value, defaultValue = { key: null, direction: 'none' }, onChange } = {}
entries.returns: { rows, sort, setSort, toggleSort(key) }. sort = {key, direction}, with none / ascending / descending directions.
notes: Call hooks at the top level of a React component. Rows need unique stable ids; input arrays are never mutated.
Compose filtering → sorting → pagination, then render with Table parts. Use selection and expansion state independently so paging does not discard other selected keys.
State hooks accept {value, defaultValue, onChange} where documented. A controlled value must be updated by its host.

entries.name: ConfirmDialog
entries.summary: “Are you sure?” done properly: the title says what will happen, the buttons say what they do, and for something that cannot be undone the safe choice has focus.

props.description: What will happen.

props.name: children
props.description: What will happen.

props.name: confirmLabel
props.description: Say what the buttons do.

props.name: cancelLabel
props.description: Say what the buttons do.

props.name: danger
props.description: Red confirm button; focus starts on Cancel.

props.name: onConfirm
props.description: Both required.

props.name: onCancel
props.description: Both required.

keyboard.does: Between the two buttons.
Same as Cancel.

notes: Avoid “OK” and “Yes”: a button’s label should still make sense out of context.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <ConfirmDialog open={open} title="Delete this draft?" confirmLabel="Delete the draft" cancelLabel="Keep it" danger onConfirm={remove} onCancel={close}>It cannot be recovered.</ConfirmDialog>

entries.name: Dialog
entries.summary: A modal dialog: it takes over the screen until it is dealt with. Focus moves in and is trapped, Escape and the backdrop close it, the page behind stops scrolling and focus returns to what opened it.
entries.description:
A modal dialog: it takes over the screen until it is dealt with. Focus moves
in (to the element marked `data-autofocus`, else the first control), Tab and
Shift+Tab stay inside, Escape and a press on the backdrop close it, the page
behind stops scrolling, and focus returns to what opened it. It is named by
its title. Use it sparingly — most things do not need to interrupt.

<Dialog open={open} onClose={() => setOpen(false)} title="Rename" footer={<>…buttons…</>}>…</Dialog>

props.name: open
props.description: You own the open state.

props.name: onClose
props.description: You own the open state.

props.name: title
props.description: The heading; also the dialog’s name.

props.name: footer
props.description: The buttons; the primary action comes last.

props.name: width
props.description: A CSS length.

props.name: dismissible
props.description: Allow Escape, the backdrop and the close button.

keyboard.does: Cycle through the controls inside; never leave.
Close.

notes: Mark the element that should take focus first with data-autofocus; otherwise it is the first control.
Smooth scrolling is stopped and the page behind is locked while it is open.
Use it sparingly — most things do not need to interrupt.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Dialog open={open} onClose={() => setOpen(false)} title="Rename" footer={<><button onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button><button onClick={save}>Save</button></>}>…</Dialog>

entries.name: Drawer
entries.summary: A dialog that slides in from an edge and runs the full height — for a filter panel or a record’s detail, where the page behind still gives context.
entries.description:
A dialog that slides in from an edge and runs the full height — for a filter
panel, a detail view, a settings sheet — where the page behind still gives
context. Everything a Dialog does for focus, Escape and scrolling, it does too.

<Drawer open={open} onClose={…} title="Filters" side="right">…</Drawer>

props.name: side
props.description: Which edge it comes from.

props.name: width
props.description: Its width, capped at the screen.

props.name: ...props
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

props.name: ...dialog
props.description: Everything a Dialog takes.

keyboard.does: Cycle inside it.
Close.

notes: Everything a Dialog does for focus, Escape and scrolling, a Drawer does too.
Under reduced motion it appears without sliding.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Drawer open={open} onClose={close} title="Filters" side="right">…</Drawer>

entries.name: HoverCard

entries.description:
A preview card for a link: hover or focus the link and a little more about where
it goes appears, and stays while the pointer is on it. Because touch has no
hover, the card must only ever *add* — the link has to make sense without it.

<HoverCard title="Glossary" body="Every term the site uses…"><Link to="/resources/glossary">…</Link></HoverCard>

props.name: title
props.description: The card’s heading and text.

props.name: body
props.description: The card’s heading and text.

props.name: delay
props.description: Milliseconds of hover before it opens.

keyboard.does: Focusing the link opens the card.
Closes it.

notes: Touch has no hover, so the link has to make sense without the card.
Linked by aria-describedby; the card is not focusable.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <HoverCard title="Glossary" body="Every term the site uses…"><Link to="/resources/glossary">glossary</Link></HoverCard>

entries.name: Popover
entries.summary: A panel that opens under a button and holds anything — text, a small form, a few links. It is not modal: focus stays where it is and Tab moves on into the panel.
entries.description:
A panel that opens under a button and holds anything — text, a small form, a
few links. It is not modal: focus stays where it is and Tab moves on into the
panel, which follows the button in the page. Escape closes it and returns to the
button; so does a press anywhere outside.

props.name: label
props.description: The button’s text.

props.name: title
props.description: A small heading inside the panel; also names it.

props.name: align
props.description: Where the panel sits.

props.name: placement
props.description: Where the panel sits.

keyboard.does: Open or close.
Close and return to the button.
Into the panel, which follows the button in the page.

notes: A press outside closes it.
If it must be answered before anything else, it is a dialog, not a popover.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Popover label="Share" title="Share this view">…</Popover>

entries.name: Tooltip
entries.summary: A short description that appears beside a control on hover or keyboard focus, after a beat so it does not flicker. It adds detail; it never replaces a label.
entries.description:
A short description that appears beside a control on hover or keyboard focus,
after a beat so it does not flicker as the pointer crosses. It is wired up with
`aria-describedby`, is dismissed with Escape, and never holds anything the user
needs to act on — a tooltip adds detail, it does not replace a label.

<Tooltip text="Copy a link"><button>…</button></Tooltip>   (one focusable child)

props.name: text
props.description: The description.

props.name: placement
props.description: Where it appears.

props.name: delay
props.description: Milliseconds of hover before it shows (focus shows it at once).

keyboard.does: Focusing the control shows the tooltip.
Dismisses it without moving focus.

notes: Wired with aria-describedby on the one focusable child.
Never put anything in a tooltip the user needs to act on — touch has no hover.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Tooltip text="Copy a link"><button aria-label="Copy a link">…</button></Tooltip>

props.name: ratio

keyboard.does: Layout only.

notes: The child is stretched to fill, so give media object-fit.

entries.name: Callout

props.name: tone

props.name: title
props.description: Replaces the default title.

keyboard.does: Not interactive.

entries.name: Card
entries.summary: A surface that groups related content, in four variants. The title is a heading whose level you choose, so the card fits the outline of the page it is on.
entries.description:
A surface that groups related content. Variants: `raised` (the default),
`flat`, `outline` and `accent`. The title is a heading whose level you choose
with `as`, so the card fits the outline of the page it is on. `interactive`
lifts it on hover and focus — put the one link or button inside it, and make
that the thing you press (do not wrap a whole card in a link).

props.name: eyebrow
props.description: The small label, the heading and the foot line.

props.name: title
props.description: The small label, the heading and the foot line.

props.name: as
props.description: The title’s heading element.

props.name: footer
props.description: The small label, the heading and the foot line.

props.name: variant
props.description: The surface.

props.name: interactive
props.description: Lift on hover and focus.

keyboard.does: To the one link or button inside it.

notes: Do not wrap a whole card in a link — put the link on the title or in the footer.
Use the accent variant at most once per screen.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Card eyebrow="Accent" title="Pick one" variant="accent" footer="Once per screen.">The red wash says start here.</Card>

entries.name: Center

entries.name: Container

entries.name: Disclosure
entries.summary: One section that opens and closes — a question and its answer, a “more detail”. The closed body is out of the tab order and the reading order, not only out of sight.

The heading holds a button that says whether the section is open; the closed
body is out of the tab order and the reading order, not only out of sight.

props.description: Controlled or not.

entries.summary: A heading in the serif voice. `level` is the HTML element (for the outline); `size` is how it looks, from the type scale — display, hero, h1–h4. New in this library.
entries.description:
A heading in the serif voice. `level` is the HTML element (h1–h6, for the
outline); `size` is how it looks, from the type scale:
'display' · 'hero' · 'h1' · 'h2' · 'h3' · 'h4'. They are separate on purpose:
the outline is about structure, the size is about the design.
Sizes are fluid tokens (`--fs-*`): never set a font size on it.

props.name: level
props.description: Which `<h1>`–`<h6>` to render.

props.name: size
props.description: The look. Defaults from `level`.

props.description: Override the element.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

bestPractices.text: One `level={1}` per page; keep levels in order.
Set a font size, weight or colour on it.

rules: Block-level; fluid type (`--fs-*`). Wraps balanced; cap very long titles with a Container or `Center`.

examples.code: <Heading level={1} size="hero">Operational platforms.</Heading>

Disclosure list with real height animation. Each row: index, title, optional
meta; the header scrambles its meta code on hover/focus, the plus turns, the
body opens with eased height + opacity (never a jump).

items: [{ id, title, meta, body }]   body: string | node
single: only one row open at a time (default true)

Hide content a reader needs to compare — use a table.

entries.description:
Before / after comparison. Drag the handle (mouse, touch, pen), press the
track to glide there, or use ← → Home End on the handle. The position is a
registered CSS variable, so clicking the track or using the keyboard EASES
the reveal instead of snapping; while dragging the ease is off so the handle
tracks the finger exactly.

props.name: after

entries.name: DragRail
entries.summary: A horizontal rail of cards. Touch scrolls natively with snap; with a mouse you can grab and fling it. The rail is a named, keyboard-scrollable region.
entries.description:
A horizontal rail of cards. Touch scrolls natively with snap. With a mouse
you can grab and fling it: drag moves the rail 1:1 and release carries on
with momentum that decays smoothly. Also: ← → buttons, arrow keys on the
focused rail, and a progress thumb that tracks position. A drag never fires
the click on the card underneath.

props.name: children
props.description: The cards. Give each a fixed width (≈ 16–22rem).

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name of the scrollable region.

keyboard.does: Scroll the rail when it has focus.

rules: The rail fills its parent; its **children** carry the width. Use cards 16–22rem wide.

entries.name: GlideTabs
entries.summary: A segmented control / tab list whose selection ink glides between tabs. Full tablist keyboard model; pass `panels={false}` when it only changes a nearby demo (then it is announced as a radio group).
entries.description:
Segmented control / tab list whose selection ink GLIDES from tab to tab
(shared layout animation) instead of toggling. Full tablist keyboard model:
← → Home End move and select, only the selected tab is in the tab order.

`idPrefix` lets the panel it controls point back at its tab:
tab id   `${idPrefix}-tab-${id}`     panel id `${idPrefix}-panel-${id}`

When nothing is a tab panel — the control only changes what a nearby demo
shows — pass `panels={false}`: it is then announced as a radio group (one
choice of several) instead of tabs that control panels which do not exist.
The keys and the gliding ink are the same.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name.

entries.summary: A typographic index: big rows that a floating preview card follows the cursor across. On touch or keyboard every row shows its own detail line, so nothing hides behind hover.
entries.description:
A typographic index: big rows that a floating preview card follows the

      "id": "phases",
      "cat": "Working together",

    {
      "id": "cost",
      "cat": "Working together",

  "type": "signature",
  "kind": "integrationAtlas",
  "anchor": "atlas",
  "railLabel": "The atlas",
  "scene": "privacy-quiet-grid",
  "minHeight": 800,
  "eyebrow": "The atlas",
  "title": "Six patterns, two at a time.",
  "intro": "Choose any two. Every row compares them: how they work, how soon the other side knows, how tightly they tie the systems together, and what each does when the other end is down.",
  "patterns": [
    {
      "id": "api",
      "name": "Request and reply",
      "how": "One system asks the other directly and waits for the answer.",
      "speed": "Immediately, if both are up.",
      "coupling": "Tight: the caller needs the other side to be up and to keep its promises.",
      "fails": "The call fails. The caller must decide whether to retry, queue it or show an error.",
      "effort": "Moderate: a contract, authentication, timeouts and retries.",
      "use": "The answer is needed now, to carry on.",
      "avoid": "The other side is slow or unreliable, and the answer is not needed straight away."
    },
    {
      "id": "webhook",
      "name": "Webhooks",
      "how": "The system where something happened sends a message to an address the other side provides.",
      "speed": "Seconds.",
      "coupling": "Looser: the sender does not wait. The receiver must accept messages and reply quickly.",
      "fails": "The sender retries for a while and then gives up. Messages may arrive twice, late or out of order.",
      "effort": "Moderate: signatures, repeat-safe handling and a way to replay what was missed.",
      "use": "The other side needs to react soon after something happens.",
      "avoid": "You cannot receive requests from outside, or you need guaranteed order."
    },
    {
      "id": "poll",
      "name": "Polling",
      "how": "One side asks again and again whether anything has changed.",
      "speed": "As soon as the next poll. Frequent polling has a cost.",
      "coupling": "Loose: the other side needs to offer nothing special.",
      "fails": "A missed poll is caught by the next one. Easy to reason about.",
      "effort": "Low, but you must define exactly what “changed since” means.",
      "use": "The other side offers no push, and a delay of minutes is fine.",
      "avoid": "Freshness matters, or there are very many things to check."
    },
    {
      "id": "file",
      "name": "Files on a schedule",
      "how": "One side writes a file, such as a spreadsheet or a CSV, and the other collects and loads it at set times.",
      "speed": "Hours, usually: whenever the batch runs.",
      "coupling": "Loose in time, tight in format: both must agree exactly on the file.",
      "fails": "A bad or missing file stops the batch, and is often found late.",
      "effort": "Low to build, higher to make dependable: validation, naming and reruns.",
      "use": "The other system only speaks files, or volumes are large and a delay is acceptable.",
      "avoid": "People are waiting on the result, or the format changes often."
    },
    {
      "id": "queue",
      "name": "Queue or message bus",
      "how": "Messages go to a broker that holds them until a consumer is ready for them.",
      "speed": "Seconds, even when the other side is busy.",
      "coupling": "Loose: producer and consumer never need to be up at the same time.",
      "fails": "Messages wait. Bad messages need handling. Consumers must cope with repeats.",
      "effort": "Higher: run a broker, design the messages, watch the backlog.",
      "use": "Bursts, many consumers, or a receiver that must never be overwhelmed.",
      "avoid": "A single simple call would do. The broker is another system to run."
    },
    {
      "id": "db",
      "name": "A shared database",
      "how": "Both systems read and write the same tables.",
      "speed": "Immediately.",
      "coupling": "The tightest of all: every change to the tables is felt by both.",
      "fails": "One system’s bad write damages the other. Every change has to be coordinated.",
      "effort": "Low at first and high ever after.",
      "use": "Rarely. Perhaps a read-only copy kept just for reporting.",
      "avoid": "Almost always. It looks easy, and it is how many systems become impossible to change."
    }
  ],
  "note": "General reference written for this site. It is not a recommendation for any particular system, and every real case has details that tip the balance."
}} />

  "title": "What are you trying to show?",
  "lede": "Say what the page needs to do and the block that suits it comes up, with the data that makes it and the usual wrong choice.",
  "intents": [
    {
      "id": "remark",
      "label": "One thing that must not be missed",
      "sees": "A note, a tip, a warning",
      "use": "callout",
      "to": "/north/blocks#callout",
      "why": "It sets one remark apart from the text, worded by kind so that colour is never the only signal.",
      "notThis": "A banner across the whole site for something that belongs to one page.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'callout',\n  tone: 'warning',\n  heading: 'An open item',\n  body: ['This section is incomplete rather than guessed.'],\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "records",
      "label": "Records people will compare",
      "sees": "Rows and columns",
      "use": "table",
      "to": "/north/blocks#catalogue",
      "why": "A table is the honest shape for records. A screen reader can say which column a cell is in, and a sortable header lets people put the rows in their own order.",
      "notThis": "A grid of cards, which hides the columns and with them the comparison.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'table',\n  caption: 'Scheduled jobs',\n  head: ['Job', 'Minutes'],\n  rows: [['Nightly export', '12'], ['Archive old records', '48']],\n  sortable: true,\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "order",
      "label": "Things in an order",
      "sees": "A sequence",
      "use": "timeline",
      "to": "/north/blocks#timeline",
      "why": "An ordered list, so the order is announced. Words such as First and Then do the job of dates, and they are never wrong.",
      "notThis": "Dates the page cannot back up.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'timeline',\n  items: [\n    { when: 'First', title: 'Shape' },\n    { when: 'Then', title: 'Build' },\n    { when: 'Last', title: 'Retire' },\n  ],\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "questions",
      "label": "Questions people ask",
      "sees": "A question and its answer",
      "use": "faq",
      "to": "/north/blocks#faq",
      "why": "Each answer is a disclosure, so a long page of questions stays easy to scan and a closed answer is out of the tab order and the reading order.",
      "notThis": "A wall of text with the questions in bold.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'faq',\n  openFirst: true,\n  items: [{ q: 'Can I reuse this?', a: ['Ask first.'] }],\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "choice",
      "label": "Two ways of doing it",
      "sees": "This, or that",
      "use": "compare",
      "to": "/north/blocks#compare",
      "why": "Columns that say in words what each side is, so the comparison does not depend on colour.",
      "notThis": "A table of ticks and crosses, which says less and reads worse aloud.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'compare',\n  columns: [\n    { label: 'Do', title: 'This', tone: 'yes', items: ['Link to the page'] },\n    { label: 'Not', title: 'That', tone: 'no', items: ['Frame the page'] },\n  ],\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "code",
      "label": "A piece of code or data",
      "sees": "Text that must be copied exactly",
      "use": "snippet",
      "to": "/north/blocks#snippet",
      "why": "It keeps every character, offers a copy button and can be scrolled from the keyboard. The colours are a nicety; copying gives exactly what you see.",
      "notThis": "A screenshot of code, which cannot be copied, searched or read aloud.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'snippet',\n  filename: 'tokens.css',\n  language: 'css',\n  code: ':root { --space-4: 1rem; }',\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "views",
      "label": "Several short views of one thing",
      "sees": "Parallel versions",
      "use": "tabs",
      "to": "/north/blocks#tabs",
      "why": "One panel at a time, with the arrow keys moving between the tabs and the panel shown at once.",
      "notThis": "Tabs for things a reader must compare, which hide one half of the comparison.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'tabs',\n  label: 'Ways to link',\n  tabs: [{ id: 'html', label: 'HTML', body: ['Use an anchor.'] }],\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "words",
      "label": "The company’s own words",
      "sees": "A statement and its source",
      "use": "quote",
      "to": "/north/blocks#quote",
      "why": "A real blockquote with its source as the caption. It is for words someone said and agreed to have quoted.",
      "notThis": "An invented testimonial.",
      "sample": "{\n  type: 'quote',\n  quote: 'Nothing moves to decorate.',\n  cite: 'Hanoryx Systems, Principle 03',\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "steps",
      "label": "A list to tick through",
      "sees": "Progress",
      "use": "checklist",
      "to": "/north/blocks#checklist",

      "sample": "{\n  type: 'checklist',\n  done: 'Ready.',\n  items: [{ label: 'The type is known' }, { label: 'The words are in the data' }],\n}"
    },
    {
      "id": "facts",

      "sees": "Labels and values",
      "use": "facts",
      "to": "/north/blocks#facts",

  "lede": "Choose the shape the information has and the page shows the component that suits it, drawn with sample data, with the reason — and the usual wrong choice and why it fails.",
  "shapes": [
    {
      "id": "trend",
      "label": "A trend over time",
      "sees": "One measure, many moments",
      "use": "Sparkline",
      "to": "/north/components/data#sparkline",
      "why": "A single line shows direction at a glance and takes almost no room, so it fits in a row, a card or a sentence. Give it a text description so the shape is never the only way in.",
      "notThis": "A full chart with axes, gridlines and a legend, when all anyone needs is better or worse."
    },
    {
      "id": "compare",
      "label": "A few values to compare",
      "sees": "Four or five things, one measure",
      "use": "BarList",
      "to": "/north/components/data#barList",
      "why": "Length is the easiest thing for the eye to compare, and a list keeps the label and the figure beside the bar, so the numbers stay real text.",
      "notThis": "A pie or donut. Angles and areas are hard to compare, and the labels end up far from the slices."
    },
    {
      "id": "records",
      "label": "Records with several fields",
      "sees": "Rows and columns",
      "use": "DataTable",
      "to": "/north/components/data#dataTable",
      "why": "When people need to find, sort and compare rows, a table is the honest shape. Headers are real headers, so a screen reader can say which column a cell is in.",
      "notThis": "A grid of cards. Cards hide the columns, and with them the ability to compare."
    },

      "use": "DescriptionList",
      "to": "/north/components/data#descriptionList",
      "why": "A term and its detail, paired in the markup and not only side by side on the screen.",
      "notThis": "Bold text and a colon in a paragraph. It looks the same and means nothing to software."

Hero: scene-backed full-screen stage with the pointer-reactive headline and,
when the page declares `hero.aside`, a signature object in the right half
(an orbit navigator, a plate stack, a miniature editor…). The aside is
code-split and reserves its space so it never shifts the layout.

entries.name: HeroTitle
entries.summary: The hero headline: each word rises out of a clipped line (staggered), then the words react to the pointer.
entries.description:
The hero headline. Two motions in sequence, on the same words:
1. entrance — each word rises out of a clipped line, staggered (GSAP);
2. afterwards the words answer the pointer (lift, swell, warm toward red).
Once a word has landed its clip is released so the lift can overshoot the
line. Touch and reduced motion get the entrance only / plain text.

entries.name: HanoryxCursor
entries.summary: The designed precision cursor: a tight core dot tracks the pointer while a reticle follows with a little lag, and grows over elements marked `data-cursor`. Fine pointers only; off under reduced motion.
entries.description:
Designed precision cursor. A tight core dot tracks the pointer exactly while
a reticle follows with a little lag. Hovering elements that declare
data-cursor="link|card|nav|redacted|audio" morph the reticle into a
context-appropriate state. Fine-pointer only; disabled under reduced motion.
No React state on mousemove — everything is refs + GSAP quickTo + classList.

rules: Fixed, pointer-events none, above everything (`--z-cursor`). No layout.

notes: Mark things the cursor should react to with `data-cursor="link"` / `"drag"` / `"text"`.

entries.name: BootSequence
entries.summary: The cinematic intro: brand and a START control, a HUD calibration with terminal lines, then the lift. Starts the ambient track inside the click when one is configured.
entries.description:
Cinematic boot / entry experience.
intro  -> brand + START control glide in
booting-> HUD calibration: grid, brackets, terminal feed, counter,
         kinetic block swipes, perspective matrix
done   -> overlay dissolves and the site is revealed (onComplete)

START is a real user gesture, so it also begins the ambient track (through
the shared AudioProvider — the navbar control follows the same status). If
the browser refuses playback the intro carries on silently and the navbar
shows "TAP TO PLAY". Skip never touches audio.

Plays at most once per session (the shell decides whether to mount it). A
Skip control is always available so the user is never trapped. Reduced
motion collapses to a quiet handoff.

onComplete fires the moment the reveal begins (so the shell can animate
the site in underneath), and onExited fires once the overlay has fully
lifted away and is safe to unmount — together they replace the old hard
cut with a crossfade.

Props: onComplete(), onExited()

props.name: onExited
props.description: Called when the overlay has fully faded and can unmount.

rules: Fixed full-viewport (`--z-boot`); the page cannot scroll while it is mounted.

examples.title: Basic
examples.code: <BootSequence onComplete={reveal} onExited={() => setMounted(false)} />

entries.name: ScanlineOverlay
entries.summary: Fixed, full-viewport CRT scanline veil. Extremely subtle, static and pointer-events none.
entries.description:
Fixed, full-viewport CRT scanline veil. Extremely subtle, static and
pointer-events none.

It used to carry a 28vh band that crossed the screen forever. That one
infinite loop cost ~15 fps while scrolling (measured A/B on the home page,
46 -> 57 fps with it removed): a large translucent layer re-composited over
every animating canvas, all the time, for an effect almost nobody could see.
Removed on purpose — motion on this site is for state, not ambience.

entries.name: SynthesisCanvas
entries.summary: SynthesisCanvas — the heavy, procedural half of the cinematic. A single canvas drives every particle/ring/grid layer for all eleven phases.
entries.description:
SynthesisCanvas — the heavy, procedural half of the cinematic. A single
canvas drives every particle/ring/grid layer for all eleven phases. It does
NOT own a loop: the parent's master GSAP timeline calls `render(t)` once per
frame with the sequence time in seconds, so there is exactly one clock for
the whole experience (canvas + DOM stay in perfect sync, trivial cleanup).

Exposes via ref: render(seconds) and a one-shot still(seconds).

entries.name: SystemSynthesisOverlay
entries.summary: SystemSynthesisOverlay — the full-screen takeover. NOT a page, NOT a player.
entries.description:
SystemSynthesisOverlay — the full-screen takeover. NOT a page, NOT a player.
Mounts already playing, owns the whole viewport (nav/cursor hidden + scroll
locked by ExperienceProvider), exposes only a minimal SKIP + a subtle system
HUD, and dissolves back into the live site on completion or skip.

entries.name: Footer
entries.summary: The site footer — a directory of the whole site, not a second navigation bar: six columns of grouped links, live section counts, the status and the legal row. Collapses to disclosures on a phone.
entries.description:
Site footer — a directory of the whole site, not a second navigation bar.
The primary menu carries Work, Systems, Development and Company; this leads to
the rest: how the company works, the guides, the tools, the trust material and
the legal documents. Six columns with named groups, a search field, a row of
the site's sections with live page counts, a strip of what is new, a legal
row, a marquee that scroll velocity pushes, a back-to-top ring that fills as
you read, the visitor's local time, and a wordmark whose letters answer the
pointer. Columns fold into disclosures on a phone.

rules: Page-width section. Six columns on a desktop, disclosures under 900px. Never set a width on it.

notes: Columns come from `footerColumns`, the legal line from `footerLegalRow`, counts from `siteSections` (see `applyNavigation`).
It shows the brand mark from `assetResolver`.

entries.name: RouteAnnouncer
entries.summary: Tells assistive technology that a new page has opened: waits for the title to settle, says it in a polite status region, and moves focus to `main`.
entries.description:
Tells assistive technology that a new page has opened.

Moving between pages here does not reload the document, so a screen reader
hears nothing unless something says so. Each page sets document.title when
it mounts (and the page it replaces resets it on the way out), so this waits
for the title to stop changing and then reads it out in a polite live region.
If the link that was used went with the old page, keyboard focus is handed to
the new page's main region, so the next Tab starts from its content and not
from the top of the site.

rules: Visually hidden; no layout.

entries.description:
Top-level frame. Owns the boot gate, scroll-lock, designed cursor, light
global overlays, navigation, and footer. There is NO global animated
background — every section declares its own scene (SectionScene). Audio
lives in AudioProvider and only starts through the explicit audio control.

entries.name: AdvancedNavbar
entries.summary: The primary navigation: a hover-intent controller and a wide full-screen-width menu (categories on the left, pages across the right). Reads its groups from the navigation config.
entries.description:
Primary navigation with an intentional hover-intent controller and a wide,
full-screen-width menu (categories on the left, pages across the right). The
menu opens only on a deliberate dwell and closes on
every dismissal path: route change, link click, outside pointer, Escape,
scroll, window blur, focus-out, and the mobile menu opening. Single-child
groups never deploy a panel — they are plain links.

Flow details:
- `revealed` (set by the shell as the intro lifts) glides the bar, then its
parts, into place — the navbar is on screen the moment the site is.
- the scrolled background is a layer whose OPACITY eases in (gradients cannot
be transitioned, which is what made it jump), with the hairline drawing
out from the centre.
- one ink indicator springs between links instead of each link toggling its
own underline.

props.description: Whether the mobile menu is open (the shell owns it).

props.name: onToggleMenu
props.description: Called by the burger button.

props.name: revealed
props.description: Glide the bar in (the shell sets it as the intro lifts).

keyboard.does: Move through links; Enter or ArrowDown opens a group.
Close the open menu and return focus.

rules: Fixed to the top, full width, `--nav-h` = 72px. Under 900px it becomes the burger and `MobileNav`.

notes: Groups come from `navGroups` (see `applyNavigation` in `content/routeConfig`).
A group with one child is a plain link and never opens a panel.

Route "current". Navigating does not cover the screen. A thin red line (with a
soft wash trailing behind it and the destination written at its end) travels
across the viewport while the old page eases out and the new one eases in, so
there is always something moving and never a blank frame. Pure CSS transform
+ opacity, no blur and no filter, pointer-events: none, one-shot, and skipped
